title: kernel-cost-aware-pad-allocator-and-slot-prioritizer
author: Priya Nair
ci_status: pass (initial run failed: unit-tests/runtime-batcher; fixed flaky allocator test; rerun passed)
release_notes: Introduce kernel-cost-aware padding allocator and slot prioritizer: reduces padded tokens by ~22% on mixed-seqlen workloads and improves GPU throughput by selecting kernel-friendly batch slots. Backwards-compatible runtime config with opt-in policy. Recommended rollout: canary on low-traffic dedicated pools.
description: Context: Large variance in request sequence lengths continues to cause padding waste and suboptimal kernel selection for our serving runtime. Prior efforts focused on bucketing and padding minimization heuristics but did not incorporate per-kernel throughput characteristics and KV-cache locality when composing slots. This PR adds a cost model that combines kernel throughput profiles, expected padding overhead, and KV-cache reuse to allocate pad budget and prioritize slot placement so that batches are both low-padding and kernel-friendly. Changes: 1) runtime/kernels/kernel_catalog.rs: new per-kernel throughput and warm-cache penalty profiles populated from microbenchmarks. 2) runtime/batcher/pad_allocator.rs: new PadAllocator that computes marginal cost of adding a request to a slot using kernel cost + padding penalty + kv-cache-affinity boost. 3) runtime/scheduler/slot_prioritizer.rs: prioritizer that ranks pending slots by estimated end-to-end token throughput and latency tail risk. 4) runtime/config/batching.toml: new opt-in policy flags (allocator.enabled, prioritizer.mode, cost_weights). 5) tests/bench/kernel_cost_profiles.rs and integration tests under tests/bench to validate throughput predictions vs measured. Motivation: By surface-driving kernel characteristics into the batch composition decision, we avoid creating batches that force the runtime to use throughput-inefficient kernels or to flush KV caches prematurely. This is especially beneficial for mixed workloads (short chat turns vs long generation) where naive seqlen bucketing either over-splits or forces large padding. Benchmarks & results: microbench logging shows per-kernel throughput estimates within 7% of observed on A100 and L4; end-to-end mixed workload (50% seqlen<=32, 30% seqlen 128-256, 20% seqlen>512) in our perf-lab: padded-token reduction ~22%, median latency improved 9%, p99 latency improved 12% on dedicated pool with conservative allocator weights. Safety & rollout: feature is behind config flags defaulted off; behaviour validated by integration tests and a canary in perf-canary automation. API/compat: no external API changes; config keys are additive. Checklist: [x] unit tests + bench tests added [x] perf lab results attached [x] docs updated (brief) [x] opt-in flagged. Next steps: gather telemetry from canaries, tune default weight set, explore learning-based weight tuning.

review_comments: Evan Brooks (2025-11-05): Nice approach—can you clarify how kernel profiles are versioned? If we change a kernel optimization in the future, do we have an upgrade path?

Priya Nair (2025-11-05): Good point—kernel profiles are keyed by runtime-kernel-version in kernel_catalog. The loader supports fallback to conservative profiles; added note in batching.toml. We also include a migration script in perf-lab to reprofile after kernel changes.
Sofia Martinez (2025-11-06): The prioritizer's tail-risk metric looks promising, but the chosen risk multiplier seems ad-hoc. Can we add a small ablation study to make defaults defensible?
Priya Nair (2025-11-06): Added bench variant with risk_multiplier sweep and included results in perf-lab notes; default set to 1.4 based on p99 vs median tradeoff.
Marcus Lee (2025-11-08): CI failed on first run due to a flaky test. Found a race in slot eviction referencing freed metadata. The fix looks good. Approving pending green CI.
Evan Brooks (2025-11-11): Approving — the opt-in config and tests alleviate my concerns about unexpected rollout impact.
